name: god-object
intent: Records what a God Object costs: one class that holds most of the program's state and most of its methods, so every other object routes its data and its behaviour through it — and the price is a single point of change and a single point of failure that every unrelated feature has to read, edit and test around.
problem: Responsibilities keep landing in the same class because it already has the fields, the collaborators and the wiring — or because its name is broad enough (Manager, System, Handler, Service, Application, Controller) that anything can plausibly go there. A new requirement now lands in one enormous class instead of one small one.
context: The smell is not the class's size but its reach. A god object references a large number of distinct types and mixes unrelated or uncategorised methods, and the rest of the program depends on it rather than on each other: the canonical description is an all-knowing object that maintains most of the information about the entire program and provides most of the methods for manipulating it, with other objects relying on it for most of their information and interaction. Because so much code refers to it, maintenance gets harder than in an evenly divided design and a change made for one routine ripples into unrelated functions. In object terms it is the analogue of failing to use subroutines in a procedural program, or of using far too many globals to hold state.
benefits: A change lands in one cohesive unit instead of rippling: because behaviour lives with the data it operates on, a new requirement touches one small class rather than a class that half the system also calls into.

Tests can be built in isolation. A split class needs only its own fields initialised; a god object demands that every unrelated attribute be set correctly before any single behaviour can be exercised, even when that behaviour uses two of them.
Dependencies become visible: each class names the narrow collaborators it actually needs, instead of every client receiving the same omnipresent object.
Failure domains shrink: a bug in the reporting logic no longer lives in the same object as the persistence, scheduling and presentation logic.
Parallel work stops colliding: two features touching different responsibilities no longer conflict in the same file and the same merge.
A newcomer can hold one cohesive subsystem in their head; a class with forty collaborators and two thousand lines cannot be held in anyone's head.
tradeoffs: Splitting is genuinely expensive and is rarely one commit. The Siemens god-class work found it needs two distinct phases that literature rarely names explicitly — planning the decomposition and actually applying it — because responsibilities inside such a class are rarely clean-cut: one method typically implements part of several of them and touches attributes that belong to several of the future classes. Their reported effort was a person-week of work for two hours of planning.

The cure is the opposite smell. Refactoring.guru notes that a God Class is frequently produced by overzealous application of Divergent Change, and the mirror image is that splitting one can create a Shotgun Surgery where a single change must now be made across many small classes. Inline Class or Inline Method first, then extract.
A half-finished split is the worst outcome: a god object plus two thin satellites, with the state still in the wrong place and one more indirection to trace.
Encapsulation, not just size, is what was lost. The fields were often public so collaborators could reach in directly; restoring accessors is usually larger than the extraction itself.

Some coupling is irreducible. Attributes accessed by more than about a third of a god class's methods cannot be assigned to any single responsibility and end up in a shared 'common' class that all the extracted classes reference — that shared core is the residue of the god object.

There are real god objects. A firmware or real-time main loop on a microcontroller legitimately centralises state because determinism and bounded memory matter more than maintainability, and a well-written game-loop manager is the deliberate version of the smell. Judge by consequences, not by line count.
quality_attributes_note: Scoring convention for this anti-pattern record: quality_attributes describe the codebase while the smell is present, not the merit of this entry, and benefits are the payoff of removing it while tradeoffs are what the smell costs (plus, where real, what removing it costs). Here maintainability and simplicity bottom out because the class concentrates every reason to change into one place; performance and scalability sit mid-range because centralisation genuinely helps locality and eliminates per-call indirection on small systems; coupling and type_safety are low because clients reach through one object instead of declaring narrow, checked dependencies.

participants.responsibility: Holds most of the system state, implements most of its operations, and references most of the distinct types. Exposes its fields broadly, so collaborators read and mutate its state directly rather than through narrow services.
participants.notes: Its name is the first warning sign: Driver, Manager, System, Subsystem or Service. UML Distilled rule 3.2 states it plainly — do not create god classes or objects, and be very suspicious of an abstraction whose name contains Driver, Manager, System or Subsystem.

participants.responsibility: Reach the god object for data and for behaviour, passing it down through their own signatures even when only one of its responsibilities is needed.
participants.notes: They should be re-pointed at narrow collaborators; each of them already knows which one.

participants.responsibility: The repositories, clients, formatters and policies the god object holds but never exposes, so their existence is invisible from any signature.
participants.notes: These are the seams the extraction exposes first, and the reason the object feels testable only end-to-end.

use_cases: Legacy J2EE/EJB entity beans: a CMP entity bean that accumulates business logic until it holds an entire subsystem — the documented source of the term's modern use.

Rails models that grow a find_or_create_user_with_valid_password helper, then a mailer concern, then a controller-facing formatting method, until the model reaches into six other models from callbacks.
An Android Activity holding view state, network clients, database handles, navigation and analytics in one class, so the lifecycle callbacks cannot be tested without inflating the whole thing.

The embedded 'GameManager' from the canonical example: managing players, game logic, rendering, input and file I/O in one class, which the accompanying refactor splits into InputHandler/GameLogic and friends.
A single ORM entity that also owns validation, presentation formatting, authorisation and the HTTP response shape, so the persistence type cannot be reused outside the web layer.

Rails/JavaScript applications whose single module-level object exports every function in the app — module scope is enough of an object to become a god object when one file accumulates the whole domain.
avoid_when: Firmware, hard-real-time loops and microcontroller targets where central state is the design and the whole program is a few kilobytes of RAM — determinism and bounded memory outrank maintainability there.
A single-pass batch job, a one-shot CLI or a throwaway prototype with a known short lifetime — the cost of splitting exceeds the life of the code.
A generated class, or an ORM/ActiveRecord model whose framework contract forces persistence and serialisation into the same type. Split the behaviour out, but the data class has to stay.
A facade over an API that genuinely is one surface — a windowing toolkit handle, a session, a database handle — provided it delegates rather than deciding, and holds no business rules itself.
A game-loop or simulation manager that owns the authoritative state and is the only writer to it; there the centralisation is the feature, provided the subsystems it calls are still narrow.
pitfalls: Splitting by noun rather than by responsibility. 'It has a User part and an Order part' is a guess; the right unit is the set of methods and attributes that never need each other.
Moving the fields first and the behaviour second. Extracting attributes that are still written from five methods just relocates the shared mutable state and makes the next extraction harder.
Leaving a ServiceLocator or singleton behind after the split, so the new small classes all reach back through one global accessor and the god object simply re-forms under another name.
Calling a bag of static helpers an extraction. Moving methods to `Utils`/`Common` removes the god object and creates a worse one, because the data and the behaviour are now further apart than before.

related_patterns_notes.facade: A facade is a narrow, forwarding face over a subsystem and holds no domain rules of its own; a god object is the same shape taken to the extreme — wide, stateful, and full of decisions. When the extraction produces a class that still knows everything, it is a god object, not a facade.
related_patterns_notes.aggregate: A DDD Aggregate is deliberately the single entry point for a consistency boundary and may legitimately be large; it is not a god object because it refuses changes to its invariants that do not belong to its boundary, and it exposes behaviour rather than state. A god object ends up holding aggregates' state by reference and mutating it.
related_patterns_notes.method-object: Method Object is the opposite move: it removes one complex algorithm from a class into its own object without redistributing state. Cited here because the protocol treats them as adjacent, not equivalent — a god object's remedy is a decomposition, not a single-method extraction.
related_patterns_notes.service-locator: A service locator is the dependency-inversion failure that lets a god object stay invisible in signatures; removing the god object while keeping the locator usually just relocates it, since clients still ask for everything from one place.
related_patterns_notes.module: Modules (namespace-level organisation with restricted export) are the cheapest structural containment for languages without real classes, and the standard first step when splitting a god object.

anti_patterns: The Manager/System/Handler/Service catch-all: an abstraction whose name contains Driver, Manager, System or Subsystem, which UML Distilled rule 3.2 tells you to be very suspicious of.
The all-fields constructor: a test fixture or bootstrap that must initialise sixty attributes before one method can run, even though that method uses two of them.
Everything-through-one-reference: every client holds a reference to the same object and none of them names the collaborator it actually needs, so no signature documents a dependency.
Methods added opportunistically because the class already had the fields — business rules accumulate next to each other simply because that is where the data already lived.
State parked in the god object because it was the convenient place, then read by everyone and mutated by everyone, so no change to it can be localised.
The god object that is also the singleton: global reach plus a global access point, so the code cannot be exercised with a test double at all.
The 'application context' passed into every domain operation — not large by size, but large by reach, and the usual seed of a feature envy in every method that takes it.
design_principles: Single responsibility: a class exists for one reason to change; a class with forty reasons is not one class, it is forty classes with a shared field list.
Information expert: put each operation on the object that holds the data it needs — the direct counter to god-object, and the same rule that makes feature envy a smell.
Depend on abstractions, and on narrow ones: a class should name the one collaborator it needs, not the object that knows everything.
Encapsulate: state that everyone mutates cannot be refactored, because there is no seam behind which to move it.
High cohesion, low coupling as a measurable pair: cohesion lives inside the class, coupling between classes — a god object maximises both at once.
best_practices: Detect before you decompose: count distinct types referenced per class and flag classes far above the project median; SonarSource-style complexity rules and IDE 'most referenced type' views surface the candidates cheaply.

Plan the decomposition before touching code. The Siemens process — clean dead methods and attributes, mark responsibilities by colour over an internal usage map, extract, then consolidate what remains into a common class — is a repeatable version of what otherwise happens as one risky afternoon.
Extract a cohesive group of methods together with the attributes they touch, never fields alone.
Use Fowler's move: Move Method/Move Field (or Move Function/Move Field) to put related behaviour together, then Combine Functions into Class when a cluster of functions keeps being changed together.

If the split makes one change require edits across five files, that is the expected interim state — inline the now-redundant classes back and try a different seam. Refactoring.guru's advice is to use Inline Class when moving leaves the originals empty.
Leave one seam for dependency injection as you go: the extracted class should receive its collaborators, never reach for them, so the tests become possible immediately.
Change one responsibility per commit and keep the build green, so a reviewer can see the god object shrink.
Guard against re-accumulation: a rule that no class may exceed the project's median dependency count, or a CI check on file length and fan-out, keeps the split from healing itself back.
sources: Robert C. Martin, 'UML Distilled: A Brief Guide for the Professional Programmer', 2nd ed. — rule 3.2, 'Do not create god classes/objects in your system. Be very suspicious of an abstraction whose name contains Driver, Manager, System, or Subsystem.'

Nicolas Anquetil, Anne Etien, Gaelle Andreo, Stéphane Ducasse, 'Decomposing God Classes at Siemens' (2019) — the planning/apply two-phase decomposition, the internal usage map visualisation, and the 'more than a third of methods' rule for attributes that cannot be extracted: https://exa.ai/library/publication/pwtcnxf78th
